analysis.one_liner: Restores the requirement for electronically controlled braking on trains carrying flammable oil.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors and died in committee without ever receiving a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In September 2018, the Transportation Department repealed a rule requiring trains hauling large volumes of crude oil and other flammable liquids to use electronically controlled pneumatic (ECP) brakes, which stop trains faster and shorten crash distances. This bill would have declared that repeal void and put the original safety requirement back into force 90 days after passage. It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work along rail lines used by long trains carrying crude oil and other flammable liquids. ECP brakes apply across the whole train at once and are designed to stop heavy trains faster and in shorter distances than conventional brakes, reducing the severity of derailments like the oil-train disasters that prompted the original rule.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have voided the Transportation Department's September 25, 2018 rule that removed the ECP brake requirement for high-hazard flammable unit trains, and restored each regulation the rule removed or amended as if the repeal had never been issued.
The requirement would have returned on a 90-day timeline after enactment, restoring the braking standard for trains carrying large volumes of flammable material.

analysis.who_pays: Railroads operating oil and flammable-material unit trains, which would have had to equip thousands of locomotives and tanker cars with ECP systems, a cost the industry had pushed to eliminate; some of that cost could have been passed through to oil shippers and eventually shippers' customers.

drawbacks.text: ECP brakes are expensive to install and maintain, and the railroad industry argued the equipment's reliability and cost did not justify the mandate; those costs would have fallen on railroads and, in part, on shippers and consumers.
The bill overturned a final rule through legislation rather than the normal rulemaking process, setting the safety standard back administratively instead of through updated engineering analysis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gain is real but concentrated: most oil-train derailments that injure people happen near populated areas along specific routes, while the compliance costs are spread across the rail industry. Honest supporters would acknowledge the industry's reliability and cost objections, but the bill simply restored a standard the government had previously judged worth imposing on these exact trains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and the session ended on January 3, 2019 without the committee ever acting on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 19, 2018 by Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The bill's only action was the committee referral; no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill was written in direct response to the Department of Transportation's September 25, 2018 final rule removing the ECP brake requirement for high-hazard flammable unit trains, which it would have nullified.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads operating oil and flammable-material trains, which keep operating under the weaker braking standards the 2018 rollback allowed, and oil shippers who avoid bearing part of the retrofit cost.

for.name: Jaime Herrera Beutler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the ECP brake requirement repealed by the Transportation Department's 2018 rule.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral: no markup, no committee vote, no report, for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Railroad industry
against.role: Operators of crude oil and flammable-material trains
against.what_they_did: Fought the ECP brake mandate for years on cost and reliability grounds, pressing for the 2018 repeal this bill sought to reverse.

against.name: Department of Transportation
against.what_they_did: Issued the September 25, 2018 final rule removing the ECP brake requirement, the rule this bill would have voided.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, no vote ever occurred, so no party split is visible in the record; notably, the sponsor herself was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have forced railroads to equip high-hazard flammable trains with ECP brakes, a cost the industry avoided when the 2018 rule removed the mandate. Its interest in keeping cheaper braking standards runs against the safety of communities along its routes.

industries.industry: Oil producers and shippers moving crude by rail
industries.note: Retrofitted braking requirements would raise the cost of moving oil by rail; cheaper transport without the mandate benefits shippers at the expense of towns along the rail lines.

Restoring the ECP mandate would have created demand for the electronic braking systems, whose benefit—shorter stopping distances on hazardous trains—coincides with the public's interest in fewer severe derailments.
